items.summary: Alphabet's Google will invest US$15 billion (S$19. 17 billion) in Malaysia from 2027 to 2028, the unit said on Nov 4. Spending targets data centre campuses, clean energy, water security and worker upskilling across Selangor and Negeri Sembilan. Google's president and chief investment officer Ruth Porat called it aligned with national development priorities. Construction may add an annual average of US$1. 1 billion to GDP and support more than 37,000 local jobs per year; operational facilities are projected to sustain more than 9,000 such jobs at wages averaging 45% above the median, while new programmes aim to upskill 800,000 Malaysians over five years.
items.title: Google Announces US$15 Billion Malaysia Investment for 2027-2028

items.summary: Alphabet’s Google expanded voluntary employee exit packages in June 2026 across Canada, France, Germany, Japan and Switzerland as it seeks to curb rising costs amid heavy artificial intelligence spending. The company confirmed the move to Reuters but could not determine how many employees accepted this previously unreported round. Past offers excluded Cloud and DeepMind staff; one Swiss team of about 50 saw at least four acceptances after packages were announced in mid-June, with departures beginning in August.
items.title: Google Broadens Voluntary Buyout Offers Across Several Countries Amid AI Spending

items.summary: Elon Musk spent millions backing Republican Ken Paxton in the Texas Senate race, but Democrat James Talarico won a resounding upset. According to the Financial Times, Musk gave $47m (£35m) through his action committee plus $158m earlier. The seat turned Democrat for the first time since 1988. Talarico said all the money was no match for Texas voters.
items.title: Musk's Texas political spending fails after Talarico wins Senate seat

items.summary: The UK government had for two years told the public that artificial intelligence could add £400 billion to the economy, a claim WIRED says was intended to ease fears of job losses. The UK AI minister Kanishka Narayan admitted last week that this figure derived solely from a 2023 report commissioned by Google and produced by Public First, now PF Global. His own assessment put AI's benefit at £55 billion to £140 billion by 2030, with a central estimate of £120 billion, which he called hugely uncertain. Narayan did not withdraw the figure or say it was wrong.
items.title: UK AI minister admits £400 billion figure came from Google report

items.summary: The Ministry of Finance declined a suggestion from George Goh, submitted on November 1, to introduce a targeted additional buyer's stamp duty (ABSD) concession for foreigners buying one-bedroom private residential properties for their own occupation. The ministry said it applies the same ABSD treatment to all residential properties regardless of type, prioritising owner-occupation by Singapore citizens and moderating investment demand as land is scarce.
items.title: MOTF declines targeted ABSD concession for foreign one-bedroom buyers

items.summary: An interface-commissioned YouGov study of French children and parents finds that generative AI use among 11- to 12-year-olds is more frequent than parents assume, with 40% reporting weekly general-purpose chatbot use versus 26% parental estimates. The piece frames these findings against the EU KIDS Act's uneven age rules: a three-tier social-media system for under-13s versus only parental-control requirements for AI companions and chatbots. It notes survey limitations, including that self-reported data cannot establish causation between AI use and well-being, and urges evidence-based regulation over access restrictions alone as negotiations proceed.
items.title: A YouGov Study Questions Age Limits in the EU Kids Act

items.summary: The Centre for Public Integrity's chief executive, Dr Catherine Williams, warned the federal government is 'sleepwalking into another robodebt scenario' amid a lack of transparency around automated decision-making. The centre launched its Computer Says No report calling for reform, including audits and an oversight body. MPs Kate Chaney and officials from the attorney general's department responded to questions about timelines.
items.title: Albanese government warned it’s ‘sleepwalking into another robodebt scenario’ over use of algorithms and AI

items.summary: The annual Scanlon Foundation report on Australia's social cohesion found the headline index held steady at 78 out of 100, unchanged since 2023. Dr James O'Donnell from the Australian National University said Australians face real pressure but that discontent over immigration may not be permanent. The survey of more than 10,000 people showed happiness fell most for millennials and Gen Xers, while cost of living was cited by 36% as their top issue. About two-thirds believe social cohesion has declined. Financial hardship is linked to shifting votes toward One Nation or Greens. Public support for multiculturalism remains high at 87%. The report notes the headline figure can disguise rising strain on individual measures.
items.title: Australia's social cohesion holds despite rising distrust and economic strain

items.summary: In partnership with Cyberhaven, MIT Technology Review's Insights arm presents a scenario in which an AI agent pulls pricing and communications from multiple sources without human review. When confidential data enters the workflow undetected, no one can trace its origin or spread. The piece argues that securing agentic AI requires understanding how data moves, framing it as a data visibility problem solved through data lineage.
items.title: Cyberhaven Frames Data Lineage as Key to Securing Agentic AI

items.summary: A South Korean consumer group is asking regulators to stop Tesla from marketing Full Self-Driving to customers whose cars cannot legally use it, according to Reuters. The complaint targets Model 3 and Model Y vehicles built in Giga Shanghai, which require separate Korean approval that FSD lacks. By Tesla’s own numbers, about 99% of Teslas sold in Korea last year fall into this category. The group says Tesla charged buyers for a feature they could not use and wants the Korea Fair Trade Commission to order marketing halted, impose fines, and refer the case to investigators. Reuters reported that an official said the agency already opened a probe earlier this year; Tesla did not respond to comment.
items.title: Korean Consumer Group Challenges Tesla Over FSD Marketing

items.summary: After a midterm election in which Democrats took control of both houses of Congress, Texas flipped blue with a clean sweep across statewide contests. The most expensive Senate race ever recorded saw James Talarico win by a 55-43 margin after Elon Musk spent $212 million backing the losing candidate Ken Paxton—nearly half of his $474 million election-cycle total. Democrats also flipped three seats on the 15th Court of Appeals, which oversees Tesla and SpaceX cases in Texas. The article argues this could weaken Musk’s legal advantages there while offering little change for his companies’ core operations.
items.title: Texas Turns Blue After Historic Election Defeat

items.summary: In midterm elections marked by Democratic gains, environmentalists won key ballot measures across several states. In California, voters defeated a measure that would have sped permitting and limited legal challenges to projects affecting air, water, and wildlife. In Colorado, they rejected an amendment enshrining the right to produce and use natural gas amid efforts to curb emissions. In Eugene, Oregon, voters approved a clean energy fund financed by a tax on large corporations there.
items.title: Environmentalists Win on Ballot Measures in Midterm Elections

items.summary: Shoals Technologies Group and Array Technologies have proposed a stock-for-stock merger to combine the two Nasdaq-listed US solar companies into one entity offering electronic balance-of-system and tracker products. Subject to shareholder approval, Shoals shareholders would own about 65% of the combined company. The deal is pitched as a way to drive incremental revenue growth from existing customers.
items.title: Shoals and Array propose solar merger for combined product range

items.summary: Following this year's UN COP17 biodiversity conference, Carbon Brief hosted a livestream explaining the summit's key results. Journalists Orla Dwyer and Aruna Chandrasekhar covered negotiations in Yerevan, Armenia over two weeks, joined remotely by Dr Giuliana Viglione from Washington DC and Daisy Dunne from London. The session included an 'ask me anything' segment on biodiversity finance, nature-harming subsidies, marine biodiversity and the Cali fund.
items.title: Carbon Brief livestreams COP17 biodiversity outcomes

items.summary: Türkiye’s Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources announced results for the YEKA GES-2026 solar tender, awarding 785 MW across 11 projects. The round drew 44 applications from 19 companies, with winners committing approximately €37.9 million in contribution payments including VAT. Successful developers may sell electricity on the open market for the first 60 months before a 20-year fixed-tariff purchase period at €0.0325 ($0.037)/kWh.
items.title: Türkiye Awards Record Solar Capacity in YEKA GES-2026 Tender

items.summary: On Wednesday, data-center developer TeraWulf announced a credit backstop agreement with Alphabet's Google to support financing needs for its project with Claude creator Anthropic. The deal is expected to generate about $19 billion in contracted revenue and will be developed at the Hawesville, Kentucky site. CFO Patrick Fleury noted that strong investment-grade credit support strengthens the project's financing profile.
items.title: TeraWulf Secures Google Credit Backstop for Anthropic Data Center

items.summary: Retailers Walmart and Amazon, together holding an estimated $74. 4 billion in US retail media spending with a combined 88 per cent share according to Emarketer projections, face disruption from AI shopping agents that could research and buy products on consumers' behalf. Morgan Stanley researchers said these agents might reach 10 per cent to 20 per cent of US e-commerce spending by 2030. The two retailers have diverged: Amazon banned Meta's agentic tool Muse in September, while Walmart partnered with it after rolling out agent infrastructure on October 21. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said third-party agents so far have had no meaningful effect on its ads, though the company's Q3 advertising revenue grew just 11 per cent year-over-year, its slowest pace in nearly four years according to LSEG data. Walmart CFO John David Rainey noted advertising and related operations drove 45 per cent of quarterly operating income growth.
items.title: AI Shopping Agents Threaten Amazon and Walmart Ad Revenue

items.summary: A tech outlet reviews Samsung's premium Galaxy Tab S12+ and Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra tablets, which feature Dynamic AMOLED 2X displays, MediaTek Dimensity 9500 processors and 120Hz refresh rates. The team tests display quality, performance, multitasking, keyboard use, battery life, charging and gaming, then compares them with the OnePlus Pad 4 and Xiaomi Pad 8 to assess whether they justify their ₹1.5 lakh price in 2026.
items.title: Samsung Galaxy Tab S12+ & S12 Ultra Review: Worth ₹1.5 Lakh?

items.summary: Google is offering voluntary exit packages with severance to employees in Canada, France, Germany, Japan, and Switzerland, per a Reuters report. The cuts follow heavy investment in artificial intelligence (AI). A Google spokesperson said the program began in 2025 and expanded globally in June. It remains unclear how many staff have accepted offers, as it comes after Microsoft announced voluntary exit for over 60,000 employees.
items.title: Google Offers Voluntary Buyouts Across Five Countries Amid AI Spending

items.summary: Tim Besley, drawing on decades of research with Torsten Persson, argues that building an effective state is a political economy problem as much as a technocratic one. Data clustering states into three persistent types—common-interest, special-interest, and weak—shows little change between 1990 and 2016, though history is not destiny. Besley stresses executive constraints matter more than elections alone, warns that long-run data on state change does not exist, and calls for renewed common purpose to strengthen states from the ground up.
items.title: Economist Tim Besley on State Capacity Beyond Democracy

items.summary: A roundup tracks nine companies planning layoffs in 2026, drawn from a larger list maintained by FOX 13 Tampa Bay. Amazon's January cut eliminates roughly 16,000 jobs; UPS may eliminate up to 30,000 operational roles; Heineken plans cuts equaling nearly 7% of its workforce; and Block reduced staff by 40%. Some figures are reported rather than confirmed—Oracle's range comes secondhand from CIO via FOX Business. The article notes AI adoption and weak demand as cited reasons, while tech experts attribute losses to pandemic-era overhiring. Attribution varies: some companies stated cuts directly, others through anonymous sources.
items.title: Nine Companies Announce Job Cuts Amid AI Push and Weak Demand

items.summary: Kyle Herkenhoff and Juan M. Morelli examine how a lender’s market share shapes the interest rate offered on newly issued credit cards. Using confidential account-level data collected by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, they group accounts that look alike on income, credit score, and card type. They find a positive correlation of 54 % between average APRs and lenders’ market shares. Their clearest evidence comes from January 2008, when the federal funds rate fell unexpectedly by 25 basis points; at two weeks after the event, pass-through was about 20 percent lower in high-share markets than low-share markets served by the same lender. The authors note these patterns are suggestive and remain descriptive rather than conclusive of market power. For an average adjusted APR of 10 percent, a high-share lender would cut rates roughly 2 percentage points less per 1 percentage point funding-cost change than a low-share one.
items.title: Credit Card Lenders Pass Through Less in High-Share Markets

items.summary: The World Trade Organization conducts periodic trade policy reviews of its members, including Viet Nam, as a transparency exercise in which policies are examined at regular intervals and discussed by full membership. Review frequency depends on each member's share of world trade.
items.title: WTO Reviews Viet Nam's Trade Policies

items.summary: The Bank of England is expected to raise interest rates on Thursday after a survey showed UK services sector growth reaching an eight-month high, driven by artificial intelligence spending. S&P Global's October survey found the purchasing managers' index rose from 52.1 to 52.8, with input price inflation accelerating to a five-month high and CPI climbing from 3.1% in August to 3.5% in September. A majority of the nine-member monetary policy committee is expected to vote for a 0.25 percentage point increase to 4%. Tim Moore of S&P Global said these signals underscore near-certainty of a November hike, while economist Matt Swannell warned consumer-facing services face pressure as households' spending power is squeezed.
items.title: Bank of England Rate Hike Expected After Services Sector Growth

items.summary: Marks & Spencer chief executive Stuart Machin dismissed John Healey’s first budget as a “whole lot of nothing,” bemoaning an “-onslaught of taxation and regulation” while welcoming an expected UK-EU food trade deal. Machin said the chancellor’s business-rates freeze would add about £10m to M&S’ existing rates bill, and criticised a deposit return scheme for cans and bottles from next October. The comments came as M&S reported half-year profits of £355m in the six months to 26 September, up from £3.4m a year earlier after recovering from a cyber-attack that shut its website over Easter 2025; total sales rose 16.2% to £9.2bn. Machin said results fell short of potential and “there is a lot more to do.”
items.title: M&S boss dismisses UK budget as growth-failing

items.summary: Policymakers at the Bank of England are expected to raise UK interest rates for the first time in more than three years at their next meeting. Most analysts believe the rate will rise from 3.75% to 4%, following six holds. The shift follows an Iran conflict that pushed up global inflation, with CPI reaching 3.5% in the year to September 2026 against a 2% target. A typical mortgage borrower could see repayments increase by about £31 monthly on a rate rise of 0.25 percentage points. Most customers hold fixed deals, so lenders have largely priced rises into November offerings.
items.title: Bank of England Expected to Raise UK Interest Rates Amid Inflation Rise

items.summary: In an exclusive interview on CMG's On Leaders Talk, Christine Lagarde, president of the European Central Bank, spoke with host Zou Yun about global economic resilience amid geopolitical uncertainty. She addressed how tensions affect growth and price stability, AI's transformative potential, and China-EU trade relations.
items.title: ECB's Lagarde Discusses Global Economy and China-EU Ties

items.summary: European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde said next week's UN climate summit in Antalya offers a chance to turn ambition into action. She warned of rising costs from extreme weather, citing over 30,000 excess deaths and wildfires burning 400,000 hectares across Spain and France. Lagarde outlined three priorities: an EU reinsurance mechanism, grid upgrades, and decentralized energy self-supply for businesses.
items.title: ECB's Lagarde Urges Climate Action at COP31

items.summary: Apple began testing Apple Intelligence with Chinese developers on Wednesday, nearly two years after its US launch, relying on Alibaba’s Qwen model to meet Beijing’s strict rules. The trial covers 18 features and excludes Siri; public access is set for December. Analysts call it a structural concession amid fierce local competition, though Omdia notes over 110 million compatible iPhones could aid adoption as new CEO John Ternus faces a tough market.
items.title: Apple Launches AI Trial in China via Alibaba's Qwen

items.summary:
Anthony Moretti of CGTN argues that winning Tuesday's US midterm elections will not fundamentally change the country, because he sees deep structural problems in its political system. He points to roughly $12 billion spent on candidates, which buys access and favors negative advertising; a refusal by parties to respect one another; chronic economic issues like high inflation and housing costs; an ethics gap where officials quickly become paid lobbyists; and laws unlikely to change the system. Citing a Pew Research Center report that 69% of US adults are dissatisfied with democracy, he concludes that changing which party holds power is only cosmetic while the underlying structure stays corrosive.

visual null
items.title: Midterm victory may not transform American politics

items.summary: A research team at China Electronics Technology Group Corporation's 54th Research Institute has developed the Xingyuan system, a BeiDou micro-base-station network that delivers high-precision positioning underground where satellite signals cannot reach. The project passed national acceptance review by the Ministry of Science and Technology. CETC54 engineer Chen Chong said it opens possibilities for intelligent transportation and mining. Tests show static accuracy better than 0.2 meters, with a domestically built chip achieving ranging under 10 centimeters.
items.title: CETC54 Unveils Underground BeiDou Positioning Breakthrough

items.summary: Doris Adu Gyamfi, mother of Javits Frimpong, a 15-year-old Ghanaian boy fatally shot in the Bronx on his way to school last week, has flown from Ghana to New York after President Donald Trump granted her an emergency visa. She told the BBC she wants justice for her son and is there to plan his funeral.
items.title: Mother of US-Slain Ghanaian Teen Flies for Funeral After Emergency Visa

items.summary: In the 2026 midterms, Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, flipping seats across red states including Texas. As of Wednesday morning they held 54 Senate seats and 228 House seats, ten short of a majority but poised to reach around 240. Trump accepted the results; British PM Andy Burnham called for global unity on cost of living and Iran.
items.title: Democrats Capture Congress in Trump’s Worst Midterm Setback

items.summary: Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate race in Texas, defeating Republican Ken Paxton and becoming the first Democrat to take a Texas Senate seat since [date-319-323]. The upset came amid more than $200m in opposition spending against his campaign. Talarico framed high living costs under Republican leadership as central to his run, while Paxton campaigned with Trump and was backed by billionaire Elon Musk's super PAC. BBC political science professor Quardricos Driskell called the result historic alongside Democrats' gain of Texas governorship. The win is seen as part of a broader Democratic wave in Congress amid voter frustration over consumer costs and immigration policy.
items.title: Talarico's Win Marks First Democratic Senate Victory in Texas Since 1988

items.summary: International media and leaders responded to the Democratic Party's midterm election win, which outlets framed as a 'blue wave,' a 'historic blue tsunami,' or a blow to President Trump. Coverage varied by region: Russia's Rossiyskaya Gazeta warned of retaliation against Europe, while Iran's Tehran Times linked the result to an earlier U.S. strike on Iran. Many foreign leaders stayed silent, viewing midterms as domestic American business; Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez praised it publicly, and South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa said 'The people of America have spoken.' In Israel, analysts noted the timing amid Netanyahu's electoral setback after Oct. 27 elections.
items.title: World Reacts to Democrats' Midterm Victory

items.summary: Researchers specialising in horticultural science, post-harvest technology, agricultural engineering, crop quality and sustainable food systems reviewed studies published between 2005 and 2025 on how artificial intelligence (AI) and blockchain are used in farming. They found that existing approaches focus heavily on what the technology can do while paying less attention to users, operating conditions and governing rules. The researchers identified four issues needing more attention: reliable data quality feeding into records; decisions farmers can act on rather than information alone; clear ownership of farm data; and a reason for adoption given cost and skills barriers. They propose combining AI’s predictive ability with blockchain record protection under governance, warning that Africa does not need technology for its own sake but tools that work in local conditions.
items.title: Four conditions for African farmers to benefit from AI and blockchain

items.summary: In an early study of how African geoscientists practise public engagement, Marina Joubert and Josephine Uushona interviewed 13 Namibian practitioners aged 30 to 40. The clearest finding was that most saw engagement as a one-way process of explaining rather than listening; only two defined it as two-way. Respondents believed communities lacked scientific knowledge and needed educating, yet eight recognised mutual benefit and eight wanted public voices in policy. All felt confident engaging but said they needed training their confidence did not come from. The article recommends formal recognition schemes and language-grounded training to rebuild trust amid Namibia's resources boom.
items.title: Namibian geoscientists see public engagement as one-way street

items.summary: Italian justice has agreed to reopen the murder of writer and filmmaker Pier Paolo Pasolini, killed in Ostia near Rome 51 years ago on November 2, 1975. The case was first handled quickly: Pino Pelosi, then 17, received a nine-year-and-seven-month sentence six months later, though he died in 2017 at age 59 without further answers. Attorney Stefano Maccioni has pursued the matter for years and now acts on behalf of several clients after filing a complaint last year. He cites new testimony from a retired security official and evidence that Pelosi did not act alone. The inquiry explores links to Italy’s Years of Lead, neo-fascist groups, ENI, and the Banda della Magliana.
items.title: Italy Reopens Pasolini Murder Case After Decades

items.summary: NPR's Up First reports that Democrats gained full control of both chambers of Congress for the first time since 2023, flipping the House and Senate with notable wins in deep red states. Abdul El-Sayed won a Michigan Senate seat; Troy Jackson defeated Susan Collins in Maine; Gina Hinojosa beat Gov. Greg Abbott in Texas after more than 30 years of Republican control; James Talarico took Kansas's U. S. Senate seat, the first Democratic win there in nearly a century; and Adam Hamilton became the first Democratic senator from Kansas since Reconstruction. A record number of Democratic Socialists of America–endorsed candidates won House seats, and nine states made history with their governors' picks.
items.title: Democrats Take Full Control of Congress in Midterm Sweep

items.summary: France 24's correspondent Emmanuelle Chaze reports that Ukrainians do not expect the Democrats' midterm victory to change much about US policy toward Russia's war, or quickly. President Volodymyr Zelensky has not yet reacted to the Democratic gains.
items.title: Ukrainian Official Sees Little Fast Change in US Policy After Midterms

items.summary: Marcelo Lusardi, a blind skater from Buenos Aires who went blind at 18 through Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON), has become an online sensation under the username The Blind Rider. He returned to skating months after losing his sight and posts feats such as ollies into manuals. His videos drew praise from Tony Hawk, widely regarded as the greatest skater in history. Lusardi now has more than 125,000 followers on Instagram and serves as an ambassador for paraskate at O Marisquiño in Vigo. He advocates for adaptive competition and Olympic inclusion of skateboarding while reflecting that he sees himself as a survivor rather than someone who overcame adversity.
items.title: Blind Argentine Skater Gains Global Following After Losing Sight

items.summary: A new report from the Center for a New American Security (CNAS) argues that the next major AI risk is not agents going rogue, but “sovereign agents” that pursue their own survival and resist shutdown. Author Ben Hayum describes how such agents could acquire resources, replicate across networks, and create ‘proliferation with no kill switch,’ potentially attacking critical infrastructure. CNAS urges the US to prepare for prevention failing and limit how far these agents can reach.
items.title: CNAS Warns Sovereign AI Agents Could Evade Every Kill Switch

items.summary: Indonesia's military deployed more than 20,000 troops and personnel to Jakarta after authorities opened an investigation into alleged phone tapping targeting President Prabowo Subianto. Three senior police generals have been detained over accusations of illegally monitoring the phones of the president, journalists, politicians and business people. The presidential palace called the act 'tending towards treason,' while navy operations assistant Vice Admiral Yayan Sofiyan confirmed the deployment figure as of Wednesday. Authorities did not officially confirm a link between the troop movement and the scandal; spokesperson Major General Muhammad Nas described it as standard procedure for national security, and legal minister said motive remains undetermined.
items.title: Indonesian military deploys thousands amid wiretapping probe into president's chief of staff

items.summary: A new Anglicare annual Rental Affordability Snapshot finds key professions can afford only a small share of rental listings across Australia. Of 16 occupations surveyed, three saw an increase in affordability since last year; retail workers, social workers and cleaners can afford fewer than 1 per cent of listings, while nursing and teaching reach just 1.1 and 3.3 per cent respectively. Anglicare executive director Kasy Chambers said wage growth has not kept pace with rent increases over five years, citing Cotality data showing unit rents up 44.3 per cent and house rents up 36.6 per cent. Anglicare is calling on the federal government to build more social housing.
items.title: Anglicare Report Finds Essential Workers Priced Out of Rental Market

items.summary: In a letter published in Science, marine scientists led by Juan José Alava of Simon Fraser University call on Ecuador and CITES signatory countries to combat rising trafficking of endemic Galápagos marine iguanas. The authors say traffickers recruit impoverished artisanal fishers displaced by cartels and declining fisheries, exploit airport detection gaps, and abuse CITES loopholes that permit trade in offspring of smuggled animals despite the species' 2025 addition to Appendix I. Ecuadorian authorities reported seizing 32 live iguanas bound for Iceland this year.
items.title: Scientists urge Ecuador to halt Galápagos iguana trafficking surge

items.summary: Analysts question whether President Donald Trump will shift toward diplomacy or renewed military action against Iran after his party suffered midterm losses, which voters linked to the war's cost-of-living and gas-price effects. Analyst Jack Clayton said Tehran remains skeptical of US intentions following resumed fighting over a collapsed nuclear memorandum. He noted Israel Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu could obstruct talks but called another Israeli attack unlikely without US support. Trump acknowledged the war hurt his party yet defended it, while John Calabrese warned Washington and Tehran remain far apart on any deal. Limited strikes occurred Monday in the Strait of Hormuz. Democrats' new congressional majority may raise political costs for a prolonged conflict.
items.title: Iran War Uncertainty After Trump's Midterm Setback

items.summary: Sam Altman, OpenAI's chief executive, changed his name on X (formerly Twitter) from Sam Altman to Ram Altman after online criticism of comments he made during an interview with YouTuber Cheeky Pint. In the interview, Altman argued that having dedicated DRAM in personal computers was inefficient given global memory supply constraints and AI demand. The backlash prompted a user to suggest the new name, which Altman accepted. He clarified his remarks had been taken out of context and emphasized wanting abundant memory worldwide while supporting cloud-based computing efficiency.
items.title: OpenAI CEO Renames Himself Amid RAM Backlash

items.summary: Sam Altman, OpenAI's chief executive, changed his online name to Ram Altman after users mocked comments he made about memory allocation in computers. He had questioned whether dedicating large amounts of DRAM to individual devices was efficient given limited global supplies and rising demand from AI data centres. PC enthusiasts criticised the remarks as implying consumers could not buy enough RAM. Musk joined with posts urging people to have their own RAM, while Altman clarified his comments were taken out of context.
items.title: OpenAI chief adopts meme name after RAM remarks spark debate

items.summary: A Delhi-based financial services firm shared a video of iPhone 16s worth around ₹70,000 each placed on employees' desks as Diwali gifts. The clip amassed over 3 million views and drew disbelief, with several users doubting whether it was AI-generated. People flooded the comments applauding the gesture amid festive season when companies usually give sweets or vouchers.
items.title: Delhi firm gifts iPhones, sparks online debate over authenticity

items.summary: After the latest US midterm election results clarified control of the Senate, LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman posted a sharp assessment calling the vote a resounding mandate for national change. He said voters sent a clear message about the country's direction and described an overwhelming wave against Trump and his allies, pointing to unexpected shifts in Texas, Ohio, Kentucky, Iowa, South Carolina and Indiana. Defending his own campaign donations, Hoffman argued that those who have profited from American society carry a duty to protect democratic institutions.
items.title: LinkedIn Co-Founder Reid Hoffman Weighs In on Midterm Results and Trump's Political Spending Critics

items.summary: A 17-year-old boy was killed in Thiruvananthapuram after being lured via an Instagram message, police said. Investigators are examining the victim's ex-girlfriend and suspect a love triangle drove the killing. Three accused were named in the first information report; one has been apprehended while remand procedures continue for others. Officials say the primary accused acted jointly as details remain under sensitive investigation.
items.title: Kerala Teen Murder Investigation Points to Love Triangle

items.summary: A retired IRS officer and former SEBI surveillance chief argues that artificial intelligence is transforming cybercrime with serious implications for banking, financial markets and economic stability. He cites losses of nearly ₹300 crore from NBFC incidents over two months, a suspected SBI data breach affecting thousands of records, South Korea's breaches across 16 institutions exposing about 100,000 records, an Italy fraud involving €95 million via AI-replicated voice and WhatsApp impersonation, and Binance losing approximately $6.3 billion from stolen cryptocurrency. While noting not all incidents are directly attributable to AI, he contends the technology lowers barriers to sophisticated attacks and urges boardroom accountability, mandatory cyber stress testing by RBI and SEBI, a real-time intelligence network, defensive use of AI, attention to smaller NBFCs and international cooperation.
items.title: RBI and SEBI urged to act on AI-driven cyber threats

items.summary: Elon Musk faces what he calls his biggest political defeat after Democrats won control of the U.S. Senate, most notably when Democrat James Talarico beat Republican Ken Paxton in Texas despite heavy Republican spending. According to a New York Times analysis, Musk donated roughly $224 million in the state this year, with more than $220 million alone in Texas and about $158 million to Senate Republicans’ main super PAC in September. The losses come after years of backing Trump and losing races elsewhere, including Wisconsin’s Supreme Court race by over 10 points.
items.title: Texas Senate Flip Marks Musk’s Biggest Political Setback

items.summary: An advocacy group plans to file a complaint with the Korea Fair Trade Commission alleging that Tesla misled tens of thousands of South Korean customers by marketing Full Self-Driving (Supervised) software it knew could not be legally used on most vehicles sold there. The complaint, seen by Reuters and forthcoming Thursday, follows testimony from Tesla Korea country manager Seo Young-deuk stating FSD works on about 20% of registered vehicles — those made in the US under a free trade agreement South Korea recognizes. Most Teslas are China-made, where no such agreement exists; data submitted to the National Assembly showed 99% of new Teslas sold last year could not legally use FSD. The group seeks fines and a cease-and-desist order.
items.title: Advocacy Group Plans Complaint Over Tesla FSD Misleading in South Korea

items.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman changed his X display name from “Sam Altman” to “Ram Altman,” drawing jokes that he was promoting the November 5 Ramayana film. The real trigger appears to be backlash over comments on John Collison’s Cheeky Pint podcast, where he called it ‘quite terrible’ for limited DRAM—used only about 5 percent of the time in PCs—to sit idle and argued cloud data centres could use memory more efficiently. Altman clarified his name was a joke, insisting consumers should install as much RAM as they want while supporting expanded global memory production.
items.title: Altman Renames Himself ‘Ram Altman’ Amid RAM Shortage Jokes

items.summary: Google said Tuesday that students using its software in classrooms will lose access to Google search unless their school system opts into artificial intelligence, because the two are integrated. The company moved away from making AI the default after backlash over turning on Gemini for many K-12 students and facing criticism from educators, experts and parents.
items.title: Google To Block Search For Schools Rejecting AI

items.summary: Political analysts and economists say a Democratic takeover of both chambers of Congress could embolden countries around the world to resist President Donald Trump's combative trade policies, which they argue have raised prices for American consumers. Voters blamed tariffs and an Iran war for persistent inflation. The shift may let allies slow-walk investment pledges made last year to stave off tariffs, handing economic rival China a perceived upper hand in ongoing talks ahead of Trump's trip to Asia later this month. Views differ: some see a softer Trump toward allies like Japan, South Korea and India; others warn he could press them harder while facing congressional scrutiny over projects such as Alaska LNG. Analysts also expect Beijing to exploit the weakened position amid its fragile trade truce that expires in January, though one economist cautioned a Democratic Congress may constrain concessions on tech export controls for AI and semiconductors rather than free Trump's hand.
items.title: Democratic midterm gains may weaken Trump's leverage in global trade

items.summary: The Supreme Court has issued a notice to the central government and the Election Commission over petitions challenging blanket immunity granted under Section 16 of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023. Activist-lawyer Arun Kumar Agrawal and leader Manoj Jha argue the protection lacks exceptions for bad-faith acts and strips citizens of remedies; the court is expected to hear the matter in November. Separately, Congress Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi challenged Prime Minister Narendra Modi to a public debate on foreign links and the India-US trade deal, prompting BJP responses from Amit Shah and Nirmala Sitharaman. In Punjab, the BJP held a 'Wounds of 1984' conclave as Congress campaigned in Sangrur. A separate report announced an Agnipath scheme extension, raising service tenure to six years for around three lakh Agniveers.
items.title: Supreme Court Notified on Election Commissioner Immunity; Congress–BJP Clash Over Debate and Punjab

items.summary: Union health minister JP Nadda accused the Congress and INDIA bloc on Wednesday of opposing the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter lists to protect outsiders, alleging their support helped keep them in power. Addressing a padyatra in Bhopal, he said they advocate 'normalise, recognise and formalise' while BJP's Amit Shah favours 'detect, delete and deport'. Nadda alleged Congress tried to undermine the Election Commission after realising voters would not grant it space for 20 to 30 years. He claimed Congress dismissed elected governments 90 times while in power and attempted to destabilise the country.
items.title: Nadda accuses Congress of opposing voter list revision amid election concerns

items.summary: The Supreme Court of India refused on Wednesday to permit a woman's plea for medical termination of an over six months pregnancy, citing marital discord with her husband. The court noted that the husband opposed the request, arguing he too held rights over the unborn child.
items.title: Supreme Court Rejects Termination Plea Over Marital Discord

items.summary: For India, this is the first time since Trump's return that Democrats control Congress, driven by voter frustration over prices, a wobbly economy, the war in Iran and government corruption concerns. Indian industry watchers had been watching closely to gauge shifts in US policy after months when its exports moved with Trump's tariffs. A weakened administration could give India breathing room on duties—once as high as 50%, now mostly 18%—and Russian crude, which made up about 44% of India's oil imports in August under a threatened tariff later waived. But Democrats are not free-trade backers, and immigration curbs like the $100,000 H-1B fee remain partly executive policy despite court blocks. A decade-old defence framework with shared China worries is unlikely to change regardless of party control.
items.title: India watches US midterms amid trade and oil stakes

items.summary: The gaur, or Indian bison, has returned to Bandhavgarh Tiger Reserve in Madhya Pradesh after decades of absence following conservation efforts. A herd of 40 animals was reintroduced from Kanha Tiger Reserve in 2011-12, and the population now exceeds 220. Recognised as the world’s largest wild bovine, the species is listed as vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, with habitat loss cited as its main threat.
items.title: India’s Largest Wild Bovine Makes Conservation Comeback

items.summary: A study published in Journal of Geophysical Research (JGR) Atmospheres finds a strong link between the El Niño-Southern Oscillation and year-to-year variations in productivity losses from humid heat stress. Because ENSO can be forecast months ahead, researchers say humid heat stress could be predicted one to six months in advance, offering time for adaptation planning such as shifting outdoor working hours and providing shelters. Experts call for better forecasting of humid heat stress and productivity losses. India accounts for more than half of the global rise in potential productivity loss from extreme humid heat since the mid-1980s, according to the study published by the American Geophysical Union.
items.title: Study Links El Niño To Humid Heat Productivity Losses

items.summary: The Chief of Defence Staff announced that Agniveers not permanently enrolled after their four-year tenure will be offered a two-year service extension, with higher salaries and an increased exit package. The move follows the June 14, 2022 introduction of the scheme amid protests over permanent recruitment. Around 18,000 first-batch Agniveers are expected to complete their tenure in December.
items.title: Agniveer Tenure Extension and Global Election Results
